items.title: The Sky Before
items.description: A large sheet of paper covered in blue charcoal strokes. At the top, a circle (the sun) with rays. Below, a green rectangle (grass). In the middle, stick figures holding hands. The child says: My mother told me the sky was blue. I have never seen blue. This is what I think blue looks like. The Teacher has pinned it to the schoolroom wall.

items.title: My Family
items.description: Four stick figures inside a rectangle (the bunker). The figures are labelled in wobbly letters: MAMA, PAPA, ME, BABY. The baby is drawn as a circle with a smile. Above the bunker, there are no stick figures outside. The child says: We are inside. It is safe inside. The Teacher says the child has never drawn the surface.

items.title: The Greenhouse
items.description: A detailed technical drawing of the greenhouse interior. The drawing shows the bed rows, the grow lights, the mushroom shelves, the chicken coop, and the bee access tube. Labels identify each section. The proportions are accurate. The child has been studying the Botanist work. The Botanist says the drawing is more accurate than their own records.

items.title: The Dosimeter
items.description: A close-up drawing of a dosimeter. The dial is rendered with surprising precision — the needle, the numbers, the click-wheel visible through the glass. The child says: This is what we listen to. It clicks. When it clicks fast, we go inside. When it clicks slow, we can go outside. The Therapist notes the child has drawn the dosimeter the way adults draw a religious icon.

items.title: The Generator
items.description: A drawing of the generator, seen from the child perspective (looking up at the massive machine). The generator is drawn as a dark rectangle with pipes and wires. At the bottom, a small figure (the Electrician) is working on it. The child says: The generator is the heart. When it beats, the lights come on. The Electrician says he has never thought of it that way.

items.title: Ash Falls Down
items.description: The entire paper is covered in grey finger-paint strokes. There are no distinguishable shapes — just layers of grey. The child says: Ash. The Teacher asked what else is in the picture. The child said: Nothing. Just ash. The Teacher pinned it next to the blue sky drawing. The contrast is devastating.

items.title: Map of the Tunnels
items.description: A hand-drawn map of the bunker corridor system. The map is oriented correctly (north at top). Each section is labelled: DORMITORY, KITCHEN, MEDICAL, WORKSHOP, GREENHOUSE, GENERATOR ROOM. The child has included the ventilation ducts as dotted lines and the water pipes as solid blue lines. The Architect says the map is 90% accurate and more useful than the official bunker schematic for navigation purposes.

items.title: The Sunday Special
items.description: A drawing of the mess hall during the Sunday Special. The long table is laden with plates (circles with food shapes on them). Stick figures are seated around the table, all smiling. Above the table, a banner reads: SUNDAY SPECAL (misspelled). The child says: This is the best day. The Chef says the drawing has been pinned to the kitchen wall.

items.title: The Chicken
items.description: A drawing of one of the three greenhouse chickens. The chicken is rendered with surprising anatomical accuracy — the child has observed it carefully. The comb, the feathers, the feet, the eye. The child says: Her name is Henrietta. The Botanist says there is no chicken named Henrietta. The child says: There is now.

items.title: Self-Portrait with Gas Mask
items.description: A self-portrait of the child wearing a gas mask. The face is mostly obscured by the mask — only the eyes are visible. The eyes are drawn large and detailed. The child says: This is what I look like when I go outside. The Therapist notes that the child has drawn themselves as anonymous — the mask erases identity. The drawing is technically accomplished but emotionally disturbing.

items.title: The Garden I Want
items.description: A drawing of a garden with flowers (red, yellow, blue), a tree with fruit, a vegetable patch, and a pond with fish. The sky is blue (the child has seen the blue sky drawing and copied the colour). There are butterflies. The child says: I want to live here. The Teacher says: This is where we are going. Someday. The child says: When? The Teacher does not answer.

items.title: The Sentry
items.description: A drawing of a sentry at the periscope, seen from behind. The sentry is hunched over the eyepiece, one hand on the focus wheel. The room is dark except for a small circle of light around the periscope. The child says: He watches so we can sleep. The General says the drawing has been pinned to the sentry station. The sentries say it makes them feel seen.

items.title: First Drawing
items.description: A single wavy line across the paper, in red crayon. The child says: Worm. The Teacher says: That is a very good worm. The child is satisfied. This is the child first representational drawing. The Teacher has dated it and filed it. The child mother has been told. She cried.

items.title: The Bunker Cross-Section
items.description: A technical cross-section drawing of the bunker, showing all levels. The drawing includes the dormitory, kitchen, medical bay, workshop, greenhouse, generator room, water cistern, ventilation system, and blast door. The child has used a ruler for the straight lines. Labels are in neat handwriting. The Architect says the drawing is remarkably accurate and has used it to explain the bunker layout to new residents.

items.title: The Bee
items.description: A close-up drawing of a honeybee, magnified. The child has drawn the compound eyes, the antennae, the wings (with veins), the pollen baskets on the hind legs. The drawing is scientifically accurate. The child says: The Botanist let me look at one under the magnifying glass. It was alive. It did not sting me. The Botanist says the child has a gift for observation.

items.title: The Radio Host
items.description: A portrait of the Radio Host at his microphone. The Host is drawn mid-speech, one hand raised, mouth open. The microphone is rendered in detail. Behind the Host, the radio equipment is suggested with abstract shapes. The child says: He talks to the world. The world does not answer. But he keeps talking. The Radio Host says the drawing is the best portrait anyone has ever made of him.

items.title: The Hatch
items.description: A drawing of the emergency hatch, seen from inside the bunker. The hatch is a large circle in the centre of the paper, drawn in dark grey crayon. Above the hatch, the word SKY is written in blue crayon (the child has learned the word from the blue sky drawing). Below the hatch, the word SAFE is written in green crayon. The child says: The hatch is the door to the sky. But we stay safe.

items.title: The Chef Cooking
items.description: A drawing of the Chef at the wood stove, stirring a pot. The Chef is drawn with an apron and a hat (the child has added a chef hat that the Chef does not actually wear). Steam rises from the pot in curly lines. The child says: She makes the best food. The Chef says the drawing has been pinned to the kitchen wall, next to the Sunday Special drawing. The kitchen is starting to look like a gallery.

items.title: The Cemetery
items.description: A drawing of the eastern field cemetery. Small crosses are arranged in rows. Flowers (crudely drawn) are at the base of each cross. The sky is grey (ash). The child says: The Undertaker takes me there sometimes. He tells me about the people. I draw the crosses so I remember. The Undertaker says the child has a natural respect for the dead that most adults never develop.

items.title: The Bunker Is My Body
items.description: An abstract drawing inspired by the hymn. The bunker walls are drawn as skin (with a flesh-tone colour). The ventilation ducts are veins (blue). The generator is a heart (red, with pulse lines). The hatch is a mouth (open). The child says: We sing the song and I drew what I see in my head when I sing it. The Therapist says the drawing is a perfect visual representation of the bunker-as-body metaphor. It has been pinned to the dormitory wall.
